overview: Eswatini’s history reaches from Stone Age pigment mining to the classrooms of Waterford Kamhlaba. Archaeological materials, school records and the accounts of working craftspeople offer different windows into learning, creativity and everyday life.

periods.title: Changing colonial control
periods.summary: The earliest map record begins before British administration was established. The National Archives describes administration by the South African Republic until 1899, followed by a British Special Commissioner after the republics’ defeat in 1902.

periods.title: British administration
periods.summary: From 1903, the British High Commissioner in South Africa oversaw Swaziland through a Resident Commissioner. Swazi institutions continued within this colonial arrangement. Executive and Legislative Councils were introduced in 1964.

periods.title: A protected state before independence
periods.summary: A new constitutional arrangement in 1967 made Swaziland a protected state with a king, parliament and cabinet. Independence followed in the next year; the constitutional change and the end of British sovereignty were separate steps.

periods.title: An independent kingdom
periods.summary: Swaziland became independent on 6 September 1968. The map’s 1960 start date belongs to its coverage of the territory, rather than the founding date of an independent state.

periods.title: Power concentrated in the monarchy
periods.summary: On 12 April 1973, King Sobhuza II abolished the independence constitution and assumed legislative, executive and judicial powers. Political party activities were banned. This changed the country’s government after independence, rather than ending the country itself.

periods.title: A royal succession
periods.summary: Mswati III became king on 25 April 1986. The African Commission’s 2006 historical account places this succession within later debates over political participation. Its account describes that period, rather than supplying a current assessment of every institution.

periods.title: The name Eswatini
periods.summary: The country adopted the name Eswatini in 2018. This was a change of name within a continuing independent kingdom, rather than a second independence or the disappearance of its people.

sections.title: A very old search for colour

items.text: At Lion Cavern in the Ngwenya mountains, people mined ochre, mineral material used for pigment, long before the modern kingdom existed. A 2024 study refined the dating of intensive mining to about 48,000 years ago. Researchers used a method that measures signals stored in sediment grains. The date concerns this archaeological mining evidence, not the age of every painted surface in Eswatini.

Ochre pieces from Sibebe carry grooves made by grinding or scoring. The same study compared the chemical make-up of archaeological pieces with mineral sources, connecting many finds to Ngwenya. Such matches help trace movement through a landscape. They do not tell us whether each piece travelled with its user, passed between neighbours, or changed hands several times.

sections.title: Leaves, fibres and a patient colour test

items.text: Tintsaba describes how its weavers prepare sisal leaves for baskets and other objects. The useful fibres are hidden inside the fleshy leaf. Scraping removes that flesh; drying turns the remaining strands into weaving material. Younger leaves provide a pale fibre that takes colour well. A finished basket therefore contains a great deal of skilled work before the first coil is made.

The maker’s dyeing account includes tea for earthy shades as well as other dye powders. Workers test a few fibres before committing a whole bundle to a colour, then rinse and dry the strands in shade to avoid fading. A little test can save a lot of weaving material. This is a described workshop practice, not evidence that every basket uses only natural dyes.

Waterford Kamhlaba opened near Mbabane on 3 February 1963 with sixteen boys. Its own history explains that founder Michael Stern wanted pupils of different backgrounds to learn together in opposition to apartheid. Parents helped build the school: architect Pancho Guedes contributed designs without a fee. This particular school’s beginnings tell a story of educational choices and practical cooperation, not of identical schooling across the country.

Waterford’s account of outdoor learning remembers geology trips, visits to rock art, hikes in the Komati Gorge and camping during the 1960s to 1980s. The landscape became part of the lesson. Outdoor education grew more formally in the 1990s, with activities including climbing, kayaking and hiking. A school day did not always mean staying at a desk, although these were organised trips, not permission to wander off.

Ngwenya Glass says its handmade glassware uses recycled glass, much of it collected soft-drink bottles. Its workshop makes drinking glasses and jugs alongside animal sculptures. The maker dates the business’s revival to 1987. An empty bottle can therefore become material for something carefully shaped and used again. The recycling claim comes from the producer’s account, rather than an independent audit of its entire environmental impact.

The same account describes schools joining clean-up and bottle-collection work, with the company providing support such as building materials and sponsorship for football teams. This links a workshop’s raw materials with school life beyond its own doors. It is an example of a particular programme, not a claim that children everywhere in Eswatini collected glass for their schooling.

Eswatini introduced its own currency on 6 September 1974, six years after independence. The first banknotes were for one, two, five and ten emalangeni; a twenty followed in 1978. The Central Bank’s history separates these dates clearly. Having a new country and having a new set of notes were different events, even though both were marked on the same day of the year.

The first 1974 coins were not all little circles. The two-cent piece was square with rounded corners, while the one-cent and fifty-cent coins had twelve sides. Other small coins had scalloped edges. The Central Bank records these shapes alongside their values. A handful of change could have doubled as a tiny geometry lesson, though its owner probably had shopping in mind.

sections.title: A village built to explain a village

items.text: Mantenga Cultural Village is a reconstruction of a mid-nineteenth-century Swazi village. The tourism authority describes guides explaining how huts are made, what different buildings are for, and the role of a traditional healer. Visitors can see demonstrations of food preparation, grass plaiting and beadwork. This is a place for interpreting history, rather than a collection of houses all surviving untouched since the 1850s.

Mantenga also presents sibhaca performances with high kicks, drumming and singing. These public shows bring movement and sound into the visit alongside architecture and craft. A scheduled performance at a cultural attraction is a particular setting for an art form; it does not tell us that every historical family gathered for the same show at the same hour.

ending.text: British sovereignty ended with independence on 6 September 1968. The kingdom continued, and adopted the name Eswatini in 2018. The end of the older Swaziland map interval is not the extinction of a people or the collapse of the modern country.
